title: The Growing Dragon of Student Anxiety & Swords for Fighting It
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart begins with Connie, an anxious student who succeeded in many Pop-Up Debates before breaking down in tears one spring day, and uses her story to examine student anxiety. He distinguishes facilitating anxiety, which supports performance in line with the Yerkes-Dodson Law, from debilitating anxiety, and notes his own rate of excused students rose from 0% to about 6%, alongside broader evidence that anxiety among young people has climbed for decades. He offers three non-silver-bullet strategies: set goals within the student's control, praise intrinsic rather than extrinsic achievement, and have students reflect on past wins. The closing return to Connie is candid about his uncertainty over whether exempting her was right, balancing the value of being pushed beyond comfort against the limits of any one protocol.
points: Not all anxiety is harmful; moderate anxiety can improve performance, so the teacher's task is to prevent the debilitating kind, not to remove all pressure.
Stuart's own data point, about 6% of students formally excused from at least one Pop-Up versus a prior norm near zero, grounds the concern in his classroom.
Grade-obsession is harmful partly because grades depend on factors outside the student's control; controllable process goals reduce that exposure.
Praising intrinsic goals, in the manner of John Wooden's definition of success, counters the extrinsic focus Twenge links to anxiety.
The Connie story shows honest ambivalence: a teacher must weigh pushing students beyond comfort against recognizing when a routine has outrun a particular student.
quotes: But here’s the interesting thing: while too much anxiety makes life miserable, too little can actually leave us falling well short of our potential. Researchers have categorized two kinds of anxiety, labeling the helpful level facilitating anxiety and the unhelpful, painful level debilitating anxiety [1, 2].

The point: not all anxiety is bad. A moderate level of anxiety facilitates performance and growth, but too much is debilitating. And that debilitating kind of anxiety is what Connie seemed to teeter on the edge of, all of last year, day in and day out.

All told, by the end of the school year I probably had 6% of my students having been excused from at least one Pop-Up through official channels (e.g., the guidance counselor). When compared to my typical rate of 0% (and when we make the reasonable assumption that there were more students struggling with this than those who went and spoke to the counselor) that is a big, troubling increase.

When goal-setting, encourage kids to set goals that are entirely within their control. “I will earn an A on my essay” is less controllable than “I will have three friends and one adult read and offer feedback on my essay,” which in turn is less controllable than “I will reread and revise my essay three times, three separate nights this week.

Perhaps the single most effective way to increase your confidence is to reflect on past successes. When you find yourself full of self-doubt, take a moment to recall (as vividly as possible) some of the goals you have achieved, and the obstacles you overcame to do it.

It turned out that she had been made particularly anxious by the video camera I was using to film the pop-up debates (I was conducting a study with Character Lab that called for the use of film) — the camera had been all it took to finally push her beyond the place she could perform, and so she broke down and ran out of the room in tears. It was one of those moments — so common in my career — where I could only think, “Duh, Dave. Nice going.
